architectural_implications.after: An explicit pipeline where every production trace is a candidate eval datapoint and every accepted eval becomes a regression test for model, harness, or context changes.
architectural_implications.before: Improvement treated as ad-hoc prompt tweaking driven by anecdote and spot checks.
architectural_implications.consequence: Requires shared identifiers linking traces to eval cases and to the specific layer changed, so regressions can be attributed to a model, harness, or context diff.
architectural_implications.observation: Agent improvement is modeled as a closed flywheel spanning run, feedback, trace, eval datapoint, and change application across three layers.

architectural_implications.after: Model choice, harness logic/tools, and context content are diagnosed and upgraded separately, each with its own owner and release path.
architectural_implications.before: Debugging an agent meant swapping models or rewriting prompts as a single undifferentiated activity.
architectural_implications.consequence: Teams need three distinct versioning and rollback mechanisms and, ideally, the ability to swap the underlying model without rewriting harness code.
architectural_implications.observation: Responsibility boundaries move: model selection is decoupled from harness architecture and context management.

architectural_implications.after: Context is reviewed in the background against real interactions and updated per user or organization, as in Hex's unified context layer.
architectural_implications.before: Context was a fixed corpus, index, or prompt assembled at build time.
architectural_implications.consequence: Context store needs per-user/per-org partitioning, change history, and a review/approval interface; unmanaged automated edits become a silent regression source.
architectural_implications.observation: Context becomes a continuously curated layer rather than a static retrieval store.

architectural_implications.after: A comprehensive evaluation dataset plus simulation environment is the definition of correct behavior, written up front.
architectural_implications.before: A PRD described features; correctness was checked late by humans.
architectural_implications.consequence: Roadmap artifacts change shape; investment moves from prose specs into environment and dataset construction, which becomes the critical path.
architectural_implications.observation: Evaluation shifts from a QA phase to a specification artifact co-owned by product and engineering.

article_ideas.angle: Reframes 'our agent is bad' as a routing decision with an explicit decision rule and a per-layer release process, using the three-layer decomposition as the routing table rather than as a taxonomy.
article_ideas.audience: AI engineers and platform leads running agents in production
article_ideas.based_on: Agents can improve across model weights, harness logic/code, or context layers.
article_ideas.thesis: Most agent failures are text and code bugs wearing a model-capability costume; teams should be forced to exhaust context edits, then harness changes, before touching weights, because each rung has a different change cadence and rollback semantic that determines whether you can attribute a regression.
article_ideas.title: Stop Retraining: The Agent Improvement Ladder Is a Cost-Ordering Problem

article_ideas.angle: Argues the product surface is proposal generation plus approval, and that 'autonomous' is a later widening of a gate, not a different architecture.
article_ideas.audience: Product and platform engineers building agent tooling
article_ideas.thesis: The deployable version of a self-improving agent today is a background trace reviewer that emits reviewable diffs to context and harness behind a human gate; the human is not a temporary crutch but the safety boundary that substitutes for eval coverage you do not yet have.
article_ideas.title: Self-Improving Agents Ship as Approval Workflows, Not Autonomy

article_ideas.angle: Follows the 'evals as PRD' claim to its uncomfortable consequence: teams that adopt the slogan without budgeting environment fidelity get guardrails that pass and agents that fail.
article_ideas.audience: Engineering managers and product leads owning agent roadmaps
article_ideas.based_on: Evals are the new PRD—they define what 'good' looks like and act as guardrails.

connections.relationship: Traces are the raw corpus: SFT filters good traces and trains on them, so trace schema and retention policy determine fine-tuning data quality.
Evals act as the guardrail that makes background, automated edits to context and harness safe; without them automation becomes unverified drift.
Both address the hard part of eval construction — generating realistic, diverse inputs — with red teaming reusing trace-derived failures as seeds.
Because harness changes are code/logic/tool edits, agent improvement inherits conventional software change control rather than model-release processes.
Per-user and per-organization text updates make context a continuously curated memory store rather than a static retrieval index.

evidence_quotes.text: You cannot improve an agent if you do not define what it is.
An agent consists of a Model (the powerhouse), a Harness (the system around the model handling reasoning, execution, and observation), and Context (markdown, files, knowledge, tools).
Agents can improve across model weights, harness logic/code, or context layers.

core_insights.generalization: Applies to any LLM system: separate the pretrained reasoning engine, the orchestration code, and the retrieved/curated text so each can be versioned, evaluated, and rolled back independently.
core_insights.insight: An agent should be decomposed into three independently improvable layers — Model (weights), Harness (code/tools/prompts around the model), and Context (text/knowledge/memory) — and improvement effort should be routed to the layer whose update mechanism fits the failure. The harness and context layers are code-and-text artifacts, so they can be changed and shipped without touching weights.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It turns 'make the agent better' into a routing decision with distinct change cadences, review processes, and rollback semantics: weight updates are slow/offline, harness changes are normal software PRs, context changes are data edits. Teams that blur these layers cannot attribute regressions to a cause.

evidence_quotes.text: Context is the easiest to update because it is just text at the user or organization level.
Harnesses are updated by looking at traces, identifying issues, and changing code/logic/tools.

core_insights.generalization: Most agent failures are addressable by editing knowledge or orchestration rather than retraining; the cost ordering should drive the order in which you attempt fixes.
core_insights.insight: The improvement loop is an ordered escalation ladder by cost: context text is the cheapest and easiest surface to update, harness logic/code is next, and model weights (SFT/RL) are the most expensive. Context lives at the user or organization level, so fixes are just text edits rather than retraining or redeployment.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Gives an engineering default: exhaust context and harness fixes from traces before spending on fine-tuning. It also implies production systems should capture context at per-user/per-org granularity so corrections can be targeted rather than global.

evidence_quotes.text: Improvement can be manual (human-driven), human-in-the-loop (background process with human approval), or fully automated.
LangSmith Engine and tools like Hex and Profound automate background review of agent traces to suggest fixes and update context.
Hex created a unified context layer for data analytics agents that reviews interactions in the background and suggests fixes for context gaps.

core_insights.generalization: Self-improving systems should be built as proposal generators plus approval gates, progressively widening automation as eval coverage grows.
core_insights.insight: Improvement loops have three automation levels — manual (engineer-driven), human-in-the-loop (background process proposes changes, human approves), and fully automated — and current production tooling sits at the middle rung, where background jobs mine traces and suggest context or harness fixes for approval.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Defines the concrete product surface to build now: a background reviewer over traces that emits reviewable diffs to context/harness, not an autonomous self-modifying agent. The human-approval gate is the safety boundary that makes automation acceptable before evals are comprehensive.

evidence_quotes.text: Evals are the new PRD—they define what 'good' looks like and act as guardrails.
Building evals is hard because it requires realistic inputs, definitions of good answers, and simulation environments.

core_insights.generalization: Any system whose behavior is probabilistic needs an executable spec; the bottleneck is environment fidelity, not assertion authoring.
core_insights.insight: Evals replace the PRD as the specification artifact for agentic systems: they define what 'good' looks like positively and negatively, and they double as the guardrail that makes automated self-modification safe. Their hard cost is not writing assertions but constructing realistic inputs and simulation environments.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Shifts where requirements live and who owns them — from a static document to an executable dataset plus environment. It also explains why self-improving agents stall: without a simulation environment you cannot generate the diverse inputs needed to detect regressions from proposed context/harness changes.

evidence_quotes.text: Traces capture exact inputs, outputs, and sequences (runs, threads, trajectories).
SmithDB: A database built specifically for agent observability, ingestion, querying, and semantic filtering of traces.
Engineering teams need specialized database and tracing infrastructure to store and query agent execution history.

core_insights.generalization: New data types create new infrastructure categories; trajectory data needs semantic, not just temporal, indexing.
core_insights.insight: Agent traces are a distinct data type — runs, threads, trajectories capturing exact inputs, outputs, and sequences — that generic application logs do not represent, and they warrant purpose-built storage with ingestion, query, and semantic filtering rather than reuse of an existing observability backend.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Determines whether trace analysis can be automated at all: mining traces for failure patterns requires semantic filtering over trajectories, which is a different query model from log search or span metrics. It also implies trajectory-level retention and schema design decisions early, since they become the training/eval corpus later.

evidence_quotes.text: Red teaming algorithms sending semantically similar queries to find agent errors.

core_insights.insight: Red teaming can be derived from production traces by algorithmically generating semantically similar queries to the ones that previously produced errors, turning each observed failure into a family of probe inputs.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Converts trace data into an adversarial eval generator without hand-authoring cases, and directly attacks the 'realistic inputs' bottleneck in eval construction. It is directly testable: perturb known-failure queries and measure failure rate as a function of semantic distance.

A feature-level rule (e.g. failure occurs only for org-specific entity names => context; failure occurs only when tool-call ordering matters => harness; failure persists across all orgs and all prompt phrasings => weights) is directly testable on trace corpora.

project_ideas.based_on: Context is the easiest to update because it is just text at the user or organization level.
project_ideas.hypothesis: A classifier over trace-derived features can predict which remediation layer (context, harness, weights) resolves a failure cluster at lowest cost, and will beat an always-fine-tune baseline on cost-per-resolved-failure without increasing regression rate.
project_ideas.measurement: Cost per resolved failure cluster and post-fix regression rate on a held-out eval suite, per arm; router accuracy against the historically chosen layer.
project_ideas.name: Layer Router
project_ideas.poc: Ingest a trace corpus with labeled failure clusters and the intervention that actually fixed each (context edit / harness PR / fine-tune). Train a small classifier on features such as cross-org recurrence, entity-specificity, tool-call ordering sensitivity, and prompt-phrasing invariance. Compare against baselines of always-context, always-harness, always-fine-tune.

project_ideas.hypothesis: Approval-gated background context edits, each carrying a per-change regression suite and a bounded blast radius (user vs org scope), achieve a false-accept rate low enough to justify removing per-edit human review for low-blast-radius diffs.
project_ideas.measurement: False-accept rate (accepted edits that later regress) versus eval-slice coverage, split by blast radius; reviewer minutes saved per accepted fix.
project_ideas.name: Context Diff Gate
project_ideas.poc: Background job mines traces for context gaps and emits candidate diffs partitioned by scope (single user, single org, global). Each diff runs a targeted eval slice before reaching a reviewer. Log accept/reject decisions and post-merge regressions.

project_ideas.based_on: semantically similar queries to find agent errors
project_ideas.hypothesis: Mutating queries near previously observed failures discovers more distinct failure classes per query than broad uninformed sampling, but discovery decays with semantic distance and rarely finds failure classes disjoint from the seeds.
project_ideas.measurement: Distinct failure classes discovered per 1k queries, for mutation vs control; fraction of discovered classes that are novel rather than variants of the seed.
project_ideas.name: Failure Seeder
project_ideas.poc: Collect failed queries from traces, generate semantic neighbors at controlled distances, run them against the agent, and cluster resulting failures. Run a broad-sampling control at equal query budget.

project_ideas.based_on: requires realistic inputs, definitions of good answers, and simulation environments
project_ideas.hypothesis: Eval signal-to-noise and RL reward validity scale with simulation-environment fidelity, and trace-replayed environments yield higher per-dollar eval sensitivity than synthetic environments.
project_ideas.measurement: Correlation between tier scores and human/production judgments; regression-detection sensitivity per unit of environment-construction cost.
project_ideas.name: Fidelity Dial
project_ideas.poc: Build one task with three environment tiers (synthetic fixtures, partially recorded state, full trace replay). Run an identical eval suite and a short RL rollout on each tier and correlate scores with human judgment and with live production outcomes.

source.title: How to Build Agents That Improve Over Time: Model, Harness, Context | Interrupt London

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Harrison Chase
  • Channel: LangChain
  • Main topic: Building AI agents that improve over time through model, harness, and context dimensions
  • Purpose: To provide a comprehensive framework and practical tooling advice for building and continuously improving AI agents. Harrison Chase, co-founder and CEO of LangChain, discusses the future of building AI agents that improve over time at Interrupt26 London. He breaks down agents into three core components (Model, Harness, and Context) and explains how to improve each dimension over time using techniques like supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, traces, evaluation, and simulation environments.

Topic Map

Anatomy of an Agent

  • Explanation: Defining what an agent is by breaking it down into three core architectural components: Model, Harness, and Context.
  • Key claims:
    • You cannot improve an agent if you do not define what it is.
    • An agent consists of a Model (the powerhouse), a Harness (the system around the model handling reasoning, execution, and observation), and Context (markdown, files, knowledge, tools).
  • Examples:
    • Models: Claude, Sonnet, Gemini.
    • Harnesses: Deep Agents, Claude Code, Codex.
    • Context: Markdown, Notion, files, knowledge.
  • Terminology:
    • Model
    • Harness
    • Context
    • Deep Agents
  • Why it matters: Provides a mental model for structuring agents and identifying where improvements can be made.

How Agents Improve Over Time

  • Explanation: Agents can improve across three dimensions (Model, Harness, Context) through manual, human-in-the-loop, or fully automated loops.
  • Key claims:
    • Agents can improve across model weights, harness logic/code, or context layers.
    • Improvement can be manual (human-driven), human-in-the-loop (background process with human approval), or fully automated.
  • Examples:
    • AI engineers manually driving agent improvement cycles.
    • Fully automated improvement loops (North Star vision).
  • Terminology:
    • Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)
    • Reinforcement Learning (RL)
    • Human-in-the-Loop
  • Why it matters: Outlines the trajectory from current manual AI engineering practices toward fully automated self-improving agents.

Improving Models: SFT vs RL

  • Explanation: Updating model weights via Supervised Fine-Tuning or Reinforcement Learning.
  • Key claims:
    • Supervised Fine-Tuning takes traces, filters good ones, and trains the model; great for simpler tasks like classification or extraction.
    • Reinforcement Learning runs rollouts against tasks, scores them in real time, and updates weights; harder to do but has a higher ceiling for complex agents.
  • Examples:
    • LangSmith Fine-Tuning (SmithTune CLI interacting with Fireworks or Baseten).
    • RL rollouts running tasks and scoring results.
  • Terminology:
    • Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)
    • Reinforcement Learning (RL)
    • SmithTune CLI
    • Traces
    • Rollouts
  • Why it matters: Shows how to choose between fine-tuning and reinforcement learning based on task complexity.

Improving Harnesses and Context

  • Explanation: Updating harness logic (code, tools, prompts) and context data (text, user memory) based on trace analysis.
  • Key claims:
    • Harnesses are updated by looking at traces, identifying issues, and changing code/logic/tools.
    • Context is the easiest to update because it is just text at the user or organization level.
    • LangSmith Engine and tools like Hex and Profound automate background review of agent traces to suggest fixes and update context.
  • Examples:
    • Hex (data analytics agent with unified context layer that improves with use).
    • Profound (synthesizing personal records from interactions with AI marketers).
    • Open Wiki (open-source project populating agent knowledge from coding repos).
  • Terminology:
    • Harness
    • Context
    • LangSmith Engine
    • Hex
    • Profound
    • Open Wiki
  • Why it matters: Demonstrates practical production tools for automating harness and context improvements.

Traces and Evals as the Foundation

  • Explanation: Traces and evaluations are the foundational data types and guardrails for agent improvement loops.
  • Key claims:
    • Traces capture exact inputs, outputs, and sequences (runs, threads, trajectories).
    • Evals are the new PRD—they define what 'good' looks like and act as guardrails.
    • Building evals is hard because it requires realistic inputs, definitions of good answers, and simulation environments.
  • Examples:
    • SmithDB: A database built specifically for agent observability, ingestion, querying, and semantic filtering of traces.
    • Red teaming algorithms sending semantically similar queries to find agent errors.
  • Terminology:
    • Traces
    • Runs
    • Threads
    • Trajectories
    • Evals
    • SmithDB
    • Red Teaming
  • Why it matters: Establishes traces and evals as the core infrastructure required for any agent improvement pipeline.

Key Points

Three Core Parts of an Agent

  • Explanation: An agent is composed of a Model (reasoning engine), a Harness (system wrapper for control, persistence, and tools), and Context (markdown, text, and knowledge).
  • Evidence: Architectural diagrams shown during the keynote presentation.
  • Practical implication: Developers must separate model selection from harness architecture and context management when debugging or upgrading agents.

Evals are the New PRD

  • Explanation: Product Requirements Documents (PRDs) for traditional software are replaced in AI systems by evaluation suites that define expected agent behavior and boundaries.
  • Evidence: Discussion on defining positive and negative criteria, expected outputs, and simulation environments.
  • Practical implication: Product managers and developers must invest heavily in writing comprehensive evaluation datasets rather than static feature specs.

Traces Represent a New Data Type

  • Explanation: Agent traces (runs, threads, trajectories) capture semantic failures and complex interactions that traditional server logs miss.
  • Evidence: Introduction of SmithDB designed specifically for querying and analyzing agent traces and trajectories.
  • Practical implication: Engineering teams need specialized database and tracing infrastructure to store and query agent execution history.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

Agent Improvement Flywheel

  • How it works: Run agent -> Get feedback (human or judge) -> See what happened (trace) -> Add eval data point -> Suggest/apply changes to model, harness, or context.
  • Components:
    • Run agent
    • Get feedback
    • Trace analysis
    • Eval data point creation
    • Agent updates (model, harness, context)
  • When to use: When designing automated or human-in-the-loop systems to continuously optimize production AI agents.

Examples & Case Studies

Hex created a unified context layer for data analytics agents that reviews interactions in the background and suggests fixes for context gaps.

  • Illustrates: Automated context improvement based on trace analysis.
  • Lesson: Agents can self-heal and improve their own context memory by analyzing past user interactions.

Profound built personal memory systems that synthesize company brand records and personal records from user interactions with AI marketers.

  • Illustrates: User and organization-level context improvement.
  • Lesson: Context updates should happen across multiple layers (user vs organization) to make agents increasingly personalized.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Adopt tracing tools to record exact inputs, outputs, and tool call sequences.
    • Start building domain-specific evaluation datasets (evals) as your primary product specifications.
  • Strategic:
    • Treat agent harnesses and context as living code and data that should be iteratively optimized using trace feedback loops.
    • Move from manual fine-tuning toward automated improvement loops combining SFT and Reinforcement Learning.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • How can we build universal judges for correctness without heavy manual domain expertise?
    • What simulation environments are required to safely test agents that perform write operations on production databases?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • Supervised fine-tuning is best for simpler tasks like classification, extraction, and summarization. (technical practice)
  • There are no managed enterprise offerings for Reinforcement Learning that match those available for Supervised Fine-Tuning. (market observation)

Notable Quotes

"You can't improve it if you don't define what it is." "Evals are the new PRD." "Traces are a new type of data."

Compressed Summary

  • Agents consist of three dimensions: Model, Harness, and Context.
  • Agents improve over time via Supervised Fine-Tuning and Reinforcement Learning.
  • Traces and evaluations are the foundational infrastructure for agent improvement loops.
  • Tools like LangSmith Engine and SmithDB help ingest, query, and analyze agent trajectories.
  • Keywords: agents, harness, context, traces, evals, fine-tuning
  • Core insight: Building agents that improve over time requires structuring them into Model, Harness, and Context, while leveraging trace observability and evaluation loops to drive continuous automated optimization.

- **Main topic**: Building AI agents that improve over time through model, harness, and context dimensions
- **Purpose**: To provide a comprehensive framework and practical tooling advice for building and continuously improving AI agents.
Harrison Chase, co-founder and CEO of LangChain, discusses the future of building AI agents that improve over time at Interrupt26 London. He breaks down agents into three core components (Model, Harness, and Context) and explains how to improve each dimension over time using techniques like supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, traces, evaluation, and simulation environments.
## Topic Map
### Anatomy of an Agent
- **Explanation**: Defining what an agent is by breaking it down into three core architectural components: Model, Harness, and Context.
- **Key claims**:
  - You cannot improve an agent if you do not define what it is.
  - An agent consists of a Model (the powerhouse), a Harness (the system around the model handling reasoning, execution, and observation), and Context (markdown, files, knowledge, tools).
- **Examples**:
  - Models: Claude, Sonnet, Gemini.
  - Harnesses: Deep Agents, Claude Code, Codex.
  - Context: Markdown, Notion, files, knowledge.
- **Terminology**:
  - Model
  - Harness
  - Context
  - Deep Agents
- **Why it matters**: Provides a mental model for structuring agents and identifying where improvements can be made.
### How Agents Improve Over Time
- **Explanation**: Agents can improve across three dimensions (Model, Harness, Context) through manual, human-in-the-loop, or fully automated loops.
- **Key claims**:
  - Agents can improve across model weights, harness logic/code, or context layers.
  - Improvement can be manual (human-driven), human-in-the-loop (background process with human approval), or fully automated.
- **Examples**:
  - AI engineers manually driving agent improvement cycles.
  - Fully automated improvement loops (North Star vision).
- **Terminology**:
  - Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)
  - Reinforcement Learning (RL)
  - Human-in-the-Loop
- **Why it matters**: Outlines the trajectory from current manual AI engineering practices toward fully automated self-improving agents.
### Improving Models: SFT vs RL
- **Explanation**: Updating model weights via Supervised Fine-Tuning or Reinforcement Learning.
- **Key claims**:
  - Supervised Fine-Tuning takes traces, filters good ones, and trains the model; great for simpler tasks like classification or extraction.
  - Reinforcement Learning runs rollouts against tasks, scores them in real time, and updates weights; harder to do but has a higher ceiling for complex agents.
- **Examples**:
  - LangSmith Fine-Tuning (SmithTune CLI interacting with Fireworks or Baseten).
  - RL rollouts running tasks and scoring results.
- **Terminology**:
  - Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)
  - Reinforcement Learning (RL)
  - SmithTune CLI
  - Traces
  - Rollouts
- **Why it matters**: Shows how to choose between fine-tuning and reinforcement learning based on task complexity.
### Improving Harnesses and Context
- **Explanation**: Updating harness logic (code, tools, prompts) and context data (text, user memory) based on trace analysis.
- **Key claims**:
  - Harnesses are updated by looking at traces, identifying issues, and changing code/logic/tools.
  - Context is the easiest to update because it is just text at the user or organization level.
  - LangSmith Engine and tools like Hex and Profound automate background review of agent traces to suggest fixes and update context.
- **Examples**:
  - Hex (data analytics agent with unified context layer that improves with use).
  - Profound (synthesizing personal records from interactions with AI marketers).
  - Open Wiki (open-source project populating agent knowledge from coding repos).
- **Terminology**:
  - Harness
  - Context
  - LangSmith Engine
  - Hex
  - Profound
  - Open Wiki
- **Why it matters**: Demonstrates practical production tools for automating harness and context improvements.
### Traces and Evals as the Foundation
- **Explanation**: Traces and evaluations are the foundational data types and guardrails for agent improvement loops.
- **Key claims**:
  - Traces capture exact inputs, outputs, and sequences (runs, threads, trajectories).
  - Evals are the new PRD—they define what 'good' looks like and act as guardrails.
  - Building evals is hard because it requires realistic inputs, definitions of good answers, and simulation environments.
- **Examples**:
  - SmithDB: A database built specifically for agent observability, ingestion, querying, and semantic filtering of traces.
  - Red teaming algorithms sending semantically similar queries to find agent errors.
- **Terminology**:
  - Traces
  - Runs
  - Threads
  - Trajectories
  - Evals
  - SmithDB
  - Red Teaming
- **Why it matters**: Establishes traces and evals as the core infrastructure required for any agent improvement pipeline.
## Key Points
### Three Core Parts of an Agent
- **Explanation**: An agent is composed of a Model (reasoning engine), a Harness (system wrapper for control, persistence, and tools), and Context (markdown, text, and knowledge).
- **Evidence**: Architectural diagrams shown during the keynote presentation.
- **Practical implication**: Developers must separate model selection from harness architecture and context management when debugging or upgrading agents.
### Evals are the New PRD
- **Explanation**: Product Requirements Documents (PRDs) for traditional software are replaced in AI systems by evaluation suites that define expected agent behavior and boundaries.
- **Evidence**: Discussion on defining positive and negative criteria, expected outputs, and simulation environments.
- **Practical implication**: Product managers and developers must invest heavily in writing comprehensive evaluation datasets rather than static feature specs.
### Traces Represent a New Data Type
- **Explanation**: Agent traces (runs, threads, trajectories) capture semantic failures and complex interactions that traditional server logs miss.
- **Evidence**: Introduction of SmithDB designed specifically for querying and analyzing agent traces and trajectories.
- **Practical implication**: Engineering teams need specialized database and tracing infrastructure to store and query agent execution history.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### Agent Improvement Flywheel
- **How it works**: Run agent -> Get feedback (human or judge) -> See what happened (trace) -> Add eval data point -> Suggest/apply changes to model, harness, or context.
- **Components**:
  - Run agent
  - Get feedback
  - Trace analysis
  - Eval data point creation
  - Agent updates (model, harness, context)
- **When to use**: When designing automated or human-in-the-loop systems to continuously optimize production AI agents.
## Examples & Case Studies
### Hex created a unified context layer for data analytics agents that reviews interactions in the background and suggests fixes for context gaps.
- **Illustrates**: Automated context improvement based on trace analysis.
- **Lesson**: Agents can self-heal and improve their own context memory by analyzing past user interactions.
### Profound built personal memory systems that synthesize company brand records and personal records from user interactions with AI marketers.
- **Illustrates**: User and organization-level context improvement.
- **Lesson**: Context updates should happen across multiple layers (user vs organization) to make agents increasingly personalized.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Adopt tracing tools to record exact inputs, outputs, and tool call sequences.
  - Start building domain-specific evaluation datasets (evals) as your primary product specifications.
- **Strategic**:
  - Treat agent harnesses and context as living code and data that should be iteratively optimized using trace feedback loops.
  - Move from manual fine-tuning toward automated improvement loops combining SFT and Reinforcement Learning.
- **Questions to investigate**:
  - How can we build universal judges for correctness without heavy manual domain expertise?
  - What simulation environments are required to safely test agents that perform write operations on production databases?
## Claims Worth Verifying
- Supervised fine-tuning is best for simpler tasks like classification, extraction, and summarization. (technical practice)
- There are no managed enterprise offerings for Reinforcement Learning that match those available for Supervised Fine-Tuning. (market observation)
## Notable Quotes
> "You can't improve it if you don't define what it is."
> "Evals are the new PRD."
> "Traces are a new type of data."
## Compressed Summary
- Agents consist of three dimensions: Model, Harness, and Context.
- Agents improve over time via Supervised Fine-Tuning and Reinforcement Learning.
- Traces and evaluations are the foundational infrastructure for agent improvement loops.
- Tools like LangSmith Engine and SmithDB help ingest, query, and analyze agent trajectories.
- **Keywords**: agents, harness, context, traces, evals, fine-tuning
- **Core insight**: Building agents that improve over time requires structuring them into Model, Harness, and Context, while leveraging trace observability and evaluation loops to drive continuous automated optimization.
